one_liner: In-process Rust/Python vector index on 2-4 bit TurboQuant codes; searches 2-5x faster than FAISS IndexPQFastScan at equal bits.
what_it_does: A flat (brute-force) vector index for Python (pip install turbovec) and Rust (cargo add turbovec). It stores each float32 vector at 2, 3 or 4 bits per dimension using TurboQuant and searches the compressed codes directly, returning inner-product scores. TurboQuantIndex addresses vectors by slot (O(1) swap_remove); IdMapIndex keys them by uint64 ids with O(1) remove and allowlist filters. Files support crash-safe incremental sync(). It is not a FAISS drop-in: the API is its own, scoring is inner product only and dimensions must be multiples of 8 up to 16,384. Ready-made stores exist for LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack and Agno.
how_it_is_fast: Data-oblivious quantization: one shared random rotation makes every coordinate follow a known Beta distribution, so the Lloyd-Max scalar codebook is computed analytically, with no training and no rebuilds. Codes are scored with SIMD lookup tables; the x86 kernel adapts FAISS FastScan's pack layout, nibble-LUT scoring and u16 accumulators, and AVX-512, AVX2 or NEON kernels are picked at run time. Since 1.1.0, indexes of 32,768 vectors or more keep bit planes and search in stages: the sign plane (a quarter of the bytes at 4-bit) gives a shortlist, the lower planes rank it, and the best max(64, 1.5k) are rescored exactly. Even before staging, the 1.0.0 whole-index scan was 3.5x FastScan at 4-bit; staging raised that to 4.4x.
when_to_use: Embedded RAG or semantic search over about 10^4 to a few 10^6 OpenAI-class embeddings (d=768 to 3072) where RAM matters: 75 MB vs 586 MB float32 for 100K x 1536 at 4-bit.
Indexes that change constantly: single add 7.9-21.7 us and remove 1.4-5.8 us, against 0.19-1.03 s per remove_ids on a FAISS IndexIDMap over IndexPQFastScan, which repacks all codes on each call.
Streaming data where a PQ codebook would need training and periodic retraining; TurboQuant's codebook comes from the maths, not the data.
Filtered queries (ACLs, time windows, a SQL or BM25 candidate set) via allowlists or slot masks.
Servers with AVX-512 VBMI and VNNI (Sapphire Rapids class) or ARM Neoverse (Google Axion), where the staged search runs and the published numbers were measured.
when_not_to_use: Hundreds of millions of vectors or strict tail latency: every query scans the whole index, so cost grows linearly; use HNSW or IVF.

Sparse, bimodal, one-hot-like or low-dimensional data: open issues #309 (recall drops of up to 65 points on sparse data) and #310 (loses to the FAISS PQ baseline); on GloVe d=200 at 2-bit the uncalibrated index scores R@1 0.550 against FAISS IndexPQ's 0.565.
x86 hosts without AVX-512 VBMI and VNNI (AVX2-only CPUs): the staged search is off and the whole-index scan runs; no FAISS comparison has been published for such hardware.
High-concurrency single-query serving with concurrent writers: issue #336 measured reads dropping 40-50% with one writer and almost no gain from Python-level threads (one shared rayon pool).
You need exact float results, an L2 metric, a network server or replication.

integration.form: crate (turbovec) plus a Python extension wheel built with maturin (pip install turbovec)
integration.dependencies: Rust: rayon, ordered-float, rand, rand_chacha =0.3.1 and statrs =0.17.1 (exact pins because they shape encoded bytes); Python: numpy>=1.20. FAISS is not needed.
integration.platforms: x86-64 (x86-64-v2 baseline; AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels dispatched at run time; the staged search needs AVX-512 VBMI and VNNI), aarch64 NEON; wheel classifiers list Linux, macOS and Windows
integration.thread_safety: Search releases the GIL and runs on one process-wide rayon pool. A fair RwLock means each write blocks the readers behind it (issue #336). sync() supports one writer per file path.

gotchas: The headline speed figures predate a recall fix. The speed JSONs were last regenerated 2026-10-04 (#552, release 1.1.0). Release 1.1.2 (2026-10-06, #562) fixed the 1.1.0 staged search losing recall on corpora whose vectors share a strong common direction (MedCPT k=10 recall 0.931 vs the full scan's 0.944, with the true nearest neighbour sometimes missing). The wider stages cost up to 3% at 4-bit and 7-12% at 2-bit (k=10), or 2-5% from k=32, and the CHANGELOG says the README figures will be refreshed later.

Harness: at 4-bit the FAISS comparator is IndexPQFastScan(d, m=d, 4), i.e. one-dimensional sub-quantizers. It runs with the default L2 metric and no refine, its version is unpinned (no benchmarks/requirements.txt), and its recall is never measured: the recall tables use IndexPQ(m=d/2, nbits=8). Most of the 4-bit gap predates staging; on x86 at one thread, 1,000-query batches and k=64, the whole-index scan takes 0.701 ms per query against FAISS's 2.518 ms, about 3.6x (derived from page data).

The staged search returns exact scores but an approximate id set. On structureless random vectors it misses most of the exact top-k. Set TURBOVEC_4BIT_PLANES=0 or TURBOVEC_2BIT_PLANES=0 before the first search to force the whole-index scan. Staging only applies to indexes of 32,768 vectors or more, with dims a multiple of 32.

Masks name slots, so any mutation, swap_remove included, silently invalidates a mask; use IdMapIndex allowlists instead. bit_width=3 is stored in 4-bit fields (issue #561), and the AVX-512 kernels are not run in CI (issue #282).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No vector-search siblings are catalogued in numerics-and-arrays; the nearest entries (Gaius.jl, hpla-rs, TriangularSolve.jl) are dense or sparse linear-algebra kernels. Compared with the FAISS incumbent, pick turbovec for a small-footprint, training-free, frequently mutated in-process index; stay on FAISS for IVF or HNSW at large scale, GPUs or L2 metrics.
verified_claims_summary: First-party runs on GCP c4a-standard-8 (Google Axion ARM) and c3-standard-8 (Xeon Platinum 8481C) over 100K normalised OpenAI text-embedding-3 vectors (d=1536 and 3072), k=64, 1,000-query batches, median of 5, both libraries timed through Python. turbovec 1.1.0 was compared with the Python faiss IndexPQFastScan at the same bits per dimension, FAISS version unstated: 3.8-5.1x faster at 4-bit (for example x86, 8 threads, d=1536: 0.127 vs 0.588 ms/query) and 1.8-2.5x at 2-bit. Recall was compared against a different FAISS index (IndexPQ, nbits=8).
status_note: Very active (1.1.2 on 2026-10-06, 376 commits, 22 open issues, 17.4k stars), but the PyPI classifier still says 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha' and the file format has moved to v8 (1.0.0 cannot read v8 files); MIT and copyable. Treat the 4.4x/2.2x figures as first-party numbers measured before the 1.1.2 recall fix, against an unpinned FAISS comparator whose recall was never checked.
